questions.prompt: Which scheduling algorithm gives the CPU to the process that arrived first?
questions.explain: First come, first served: a simple FIFO queue.

questions.prompt: What is the convoy effect?
options: Short processes waiting behind a long one in FCFS
questions.explain: A long CPU burst at the head of the queue delays everyone behind it, so the average waiting time grows.

questions.prompt: Which algorithm gives the minimum average waiting time?
questions.explain: Shortest job first is optimal for the average waiting time (if the burst lengths are known).

questions.prompt: What is a cooperative (non-preemptive) scheduler?
options: One that never changes the priorities
One that only chooses another process when the running one waits or ends
One that shares the CPU in equal slices
questions.explain: A preemptive scheduler can also take the CPU away from a running process (a time slice ends, a better process arrives).

questions.prompt: The time a process spends in the ready queue is its {{0}} time.
questions.explain: Turnaround time is from arrival to finish; waiting time is only the time spent ready but not running.

questions.prompt: For a process with one CPU burst and no I/O, turnaround time equals:
questions.explain: Turnaround = finish - arrival = time waiting + time running.

questions.prompt: A round-robin scheduler with a VERY large quantum behaves like:
questions.explain: Nobody is ever preempted, so processes run to the end in arrival order.

questions.prompt: Priority scheduling can leave a low-priority process without CPU forever. What is that problem and its cure?
options: The convoy effect, solved with round robin
questions.explain: Aging raises the priority of processes that have waited a long time.

questions.prompt: FCFS with bursts P1 = 24, P2 = 3, P3 = 3 ms, all arriving at time 0 in that order. What is the average waiting time?
questions.explain: P1 waits 0, P2 waits 24, P3 waits 27: (0 + 24 + 27) / 3 = 17 ms. In the order 3, 3, 24 it would be 3 ms: the convoy effect.

questions.prompt: The same three processes arrive in the order P2 = 3, P3 = 3, P1 = 24 (all at time 0). What is the average waiting time with FCFS?
questions.explain: They wait 0, 3 and 6 ms: (0 + 3 + 6) / 3 = 3 ms.

questions.prompt: Cooperative SJF with P1 (arrives 0, burst 7), P2 (2, 4), P3 (4, 1), P4 (5, 4). Which process runs right after P1 finishes at time 7?
questions.explain: At time 7 the ready processes are P2 (4), P3 (1) and P4 (4): the shortest is P3.

questions.prompt: Cooperative SJF on that same set: what is the average waiting time?
questions.explain: The waits are 0, 6, 3 and 7: 16 / 4 = 4 ms.

questions.prompt: Preemptive SJF (shortest remaining time) on the same set: which process is running at time 4?
questions.explain: At time 4, P3 arrives with a burst of 1, less than what P1 (5) and P2 (2) have left, so it takes the CPU.

questions.prompt: Preemptive SJF on that set: what is the average waiting time?
questions.explain: The waits are 9, 1, 0 and 2: 12 / 4 = 3 ms, better than the cooperative 4 ms.

questions.prompt: Round robin, quantum 20 ms. P1 = 53, P2 = 17, P3 = 68, P4 = 24 (all arrive at 0). What is the waiting time of P2?
questions.explain: P1 runs 0-20, then P2 runs 20-37 and finishes: it waited 20 ms (its turnaround is 37 and its burst is 17).

questions.prompt: Same system: what is the average waiting time?
questions.explain: The waits are 81, 20, 94 and 97: 292 / 4 = 73 ms.

questions.prompt: Round robin, quantum 4 ms, processes P1 = 10, P2 = 3, P3 = 5 (all arrive at 0). Put the CPU slices in order.
questions.explain: P2 finishes in its first slice (3 < 4). P3 needs two slices and P1 three. The finish times are 18, 7 and 16.

questions.prompt: In that round-robin schedule, what is the waiting time of P3 (burst 5)?
questions.explain: P3 finishes at 16 and runs for 5 ms, so it waited 16 - 5 = 11 ms.

questions.prompt: Match each algorithm with its main idea.
pairs: equal time slices in a circular queue
processes move between queues with different algorithms
questions.explain: These are the algorithms of the topic.

questions.prompt: In SJF the next burst is estimated as tau(n+1) = alpha * t(n) + (1 - alpha) * tau(n). With alpha = 1 the estimate is just the {{0}} real burst.
questions.explain: alpha = 1 forgets the history; alpha = 0 ignores the new measurements and keeps the old estimate.

questions.prompt: With alpha = 0.5, a previous estimate tau = 10 and a real burst t = 6, what is the next estimate?
Which scheduler decides which new processes enter the ready queue?
questions.explain: The long-term scheduler controls the degree of multiprogramming; it runs rarely, so it can be slow.

questions.prompt: What is the cost of a context switch?
options: Time in which the CPU does no useful work
questions.explain: Too many switches (a tiny quantum) waste CPU time.

questions.prompt: Is each scheduling policy preemptive or cooperative?
questions.explain: Preemptive policies can take the CPU from a running process; cooperative ones wait until it ends or blocks.

questions.prompt: A system has three queues: queue 0 is round robin with quantum 20, queue 1 round robin with quantum 40 and queue 2 FCFS. A new process enters queue 0. It uses its whole quantum without finishing. Where does it go?
questions.explain: In multilevel feedback queues a process that exhausts its quantum is demoted to the next queue.

questions.prompt: What is the main purpose of multilevel feedback queues?
options: To keep short and interactive processes in the higher-priority queues while long CPU-bound ones sink
questions.explain: A process that uses little CPU stays up; one that always uses its whole quantum drops.
